docs.nardy.component: A POINT IS A PILE WITH A LAW, and that is the whole of what this page adds.
The chess page turned the desk into places: sixty-four of them, each one man wide, and a man is
on a square or on the next. A nardy point is a place of the other kind — a COLUMN. It takes a
checker of its own colour, or any checker when it is empty; it stands them one over the next from
the rim toward the middle; and when the column would run past the point (fifteen on the head, at
the start), it squeezes them evenly rather than spilling them. All three are the point's own
data: an accept rule, a `pileLayout`, and the layout's notion of where the NEXT seat is.
A hand takes a column the way a hand takes a run of cards: the checker it touched and every one
above it, the touched one being the grip. The picture of where the column lands stands on top
of the pile that is already there — the point's own layout is asked where one more would go, so
the picture and the landing can never disagree.
THE DICE ARE THE SECOND HALF. A die thrown beside the board stays in the band it was thrown in;
a die thrown on the board stays on the board; and while a hand carries a die it crosses the edge
freely. The wall is the throw's and never the hand's, decided at the moment of release.
docs.nardy.scene: LONG NARDY — one board, two people, no rules.
Both heads are set: fifteen white on 24, fifteen black on 12, each squeezed into a point five
checkers long. Lift the bottom checker of a column and the whole column comes with it; lift one
in the middle and everything above it comes. Aim at a point and it lights, and the dashed picture
stands where the column will lie — on top of what is there. A point of the other colour refuses,
Off the points the felt takes anything anywhere: a checker beside the board lies where the hand
left it, which is what a real table does. Flick a die and it flies inside the walls of wherever
it was let go: the board, or the band beside it.
NO RULES, on purpose. Whose turn it is, how far a die lets a checker go, when a checker may
leave — those are the game, and this shelf is the desk. Two people at one board are trusted with
the rules exactly as they are at a real one.
docs.nardy.avatars: THE SAME BOARD WITH THE TWO PLAYERS DRAWN BESIDE IT.
The cursor says what a hand is doing and says nothing while it is still, so a board with a quiet
opponent is a board with one player at it. The disc is the other half of the message, and where
it stands is read out of that player's own camera: pan the top screen and their disc travels the
felt on the bottom one, which is exactly what 'I am looking over here now' is.
The state is on the disc. Switch to another tab and both go quiet with a muted mark. Lift a
column of checkers and the holder's disc takes a ring, which is the one thing everybody else is
No hands here, and that is what a board IS: a patch of felt a player owns is a place, and on a
board every place belongs to the game rather than to anybody sitting at it.
Turn the avatars knob off and the board is the scene above.
